job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: In a bustling city workshop, an electrician is setting up a display of decorative lights. He connects two identical bulbs in a parallel circuit to a 12-volt battery. A curious apprentice asks if the bulb closer to the positive terminal will glow brighter, but the electrician explains that the potential difference across each branch remains exactly 12 volts. He then demonstrates that adding a second bulb in parallel actually decreases the total resistance of the circuit, allowing more current to flow from the source. The apprentice notices a thin copper wire connecting the components and wonders if it has zero resistance. The electrician clarifies that while copper is an excellent conductor, it still possesses a small amount of resistance, which causes it to heat up when a high current passes through. Finally, he explains that current is not 'consumed' by the bulbs; the amount of charge flowing into a bulb is exactly equal to the amount flowing out. The electrician emphasizes that electricity is a continuous flow, and the battery acts as a pump, providing the energy needed to maintain the potential difference across the circuit components regardless of the path taken.

items.evidence: He then demonstrates that adding a second bulb in parallel actually decreases the total resistance of the circuit, allowing more current to flow from the source.
items.q: An electrician adds one more bulb in parallel. What happens to the current drawn from the battery?
options: It rises, as total resistance falls
It stays the same, as the battery is fixed
It falls, as total resistance rises
It splits, so the battery gives less
items.explain: A parallel bulb lowers total resistance, so the battery supplies more current.

wrong.why: thinks a battery always gives the same current
thinks more parallel resistors raise total resistance
thinks the battery's supply is divided among branches

items.evidence: A curious apprentice asks if the bulb closer to the positive terminal will glow brighter, but the electrician explains that the potential difference across each branch remains exactly 12 volts.
items.q: Two identical bulbs are in parallel on a battery. Why do they glow equally bright?
options: Each gets the same voltage across it
Each gets half of the battery voltage
The nearer bulb gets the current first
Each bulb has half the resistance
items.explain: Each branch has the full 12 volts across it, so identical bulbs glow equally.

wrong.why: thinks battery voltage is divided among branches
thinks the bulb nearer the terminal gets current first
invents a resistance change not in the passage

items.evidence: The electrician clarifies that while copper is an excellent conductor, it still possesses a small amount of resistance, which causes it to heat up when a high current passes through.
items.q: Why can a thin copper wire become warm when a large current passes?
options: Copper has no resistance at all
Copper is a very poor conductor
Copper stores charge from the battery
items.explain: Copper still has a small resistance, so a high current heats it up.

wrong.why: mixes up low resistance with a poor conductor
thinks wires keep charge inside them

items.evidence: Finally, he explains that current is not 'consumed' by the bulbs; the amount of charge flowing into a bulb is exactly equal to the amount flowing out.
items.q: An ammeter measures 0.5 A of current entering a bulb. What will it read leaving the bulb?
options: Less than 0.5 A, as the bulb uses it
More than 0.5 A, as the bulb adds some
Zero, as the bulb glows by using it all
items.explain: Current is not consumed; the charge flowing out of a bulb equals the charge flowing in.

wrong.why: thinks the bulb uses up some current
thinks a bulb creates extra current
thinks the bulb consumes all the current
